props.title: One Body Too Many
props.initialSlug: Insurance agent guards corpse in spooky mansion

sections.content: One Body Too Many perfectly captures the intersection of horror-comedy and murder mystery that flourished in the 1940s. Starring Jack Haley (famous as the Tin Man in The Wizard of Oz (1939)), this delightfully odd film follows an insurance salesman trapped in a spooky mansion during the reading of an eccentric millionaire's will. It shares DNA with similar "old dark house" comedies like The Cat and the Canary (1939) and The Ghost Breakers (1940), blending genuine chills with slapstick humor and witty dialogue.

sections.content: The film's director, Frank McDonald, was a B-movie specialist who understood how to maximize limited budgets through atmospheric lighting and creative camera angles. One Body Too Many makes excellent use of its mansion setting, creating genuine tension while never losing its comedic edge. The plot device of a corpse that must remain unburied until a specific astronomical event occurs adds a clever ticking clock element similar to The Black Cat (1941) and Night of Terror (1933).

Jack Haley's performance as the bumbling insurance salesman Albert Tuttle shows his range beyond his iconic Oz role. His physical comedy skills shine in sequences involving secret passages and mysterious disappearances, reminiscent of Bob Hope's work in The Ghost Breakers (1940). The supporting cast includes genre veterans like Bela Lugosi, playing against type as a suspicious butler, adding another layer of meta-comedy for horror fans. SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence

sections.content: The film's influence can be seen in later horror-comedies that play with genre conventions, from Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein (1948) to modern takes like Knives Out (2019). Its blend of genuine mystery elements with comedic setpieces created a template that many films would follow. The "reading of the will" plot device became a staple of mystery comedies, perfectly executed in later films like Murder by Death (1976).
